newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russian PM to Belgium aiming for new relationship.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM to Belgium aiming for new relationship.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin arrived in Brussels on Thursday for a two-day visit to seek stronger relations with the European Union a day after the 15-nation bloc named the six states it hopes to bring into the club.

"We are starting to have interests in common...This visit should give our dialogue a new format that we want to make permanent," Chernomyrdin said in an interview with the newspaper Le Soir published prior to his arrival.

Russia has already established a special relationship with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation through the NATO-Russia Council but remains uneasy with the alliance's plans, also announced this month, to bring in former Soviet satellites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
On Wednesday the European Commission named Cyprus and former Soviet satellites Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovenia and Estonia as the leading contenders to join the EU.

Chernomyrdin said in the Le Soir interview that the principal vehicle for improved and strengthened links with the EU was the partnership and cooperation accord which lays out a framework for deeper trade and diplomatic ties between the two.

But, despite evident progress at the EU-Russia summit in Moscow in March, Moscow is known to be less than happy with the workings of the agreement after the bloc slapped anti-dumping duties on exports of Russian steel.

"The important thing today is to eliminate the anti-dumping measures that are hitting Russian goods," Chernomyrdin told the paper. "It is time to recognise that the Russian economy is a market economy as the private sector represents 70 percent."
Chernomyrdin will hold talks on Friday with European Commission President Jacques Santer and several other commissioners.

The two sides will tackle a range of trade and economic questions, including Russia's inefficient customs controls, its bid for membership in the World Trade Organisation and its investment climate, Commission spokeswoman Lousewies van der Laan told reporters.

They will also discuss possible new cooperation in areas including science and technology, education, space and information technology and 1998 priorities for the EU's TACIS development aid programme for the ex-Soviet Union, she said.

Chernomyrdin told Le Soir that one of the biggest problems between Russia and the European Union was the fears of the country's West European competitors, but that for a variety of reasons Russia did have a competitive advantage in a number of areas.
"Our natural advantages must not be used as a pretext to impose blocks on Russian products entering the European market," he was quoted as saying.
He added that Russia wanted foreign investment and wanted to try to calm worries about stability and security for investors.

He shrugged off complaints by the defence minister that President Boris Yeltsin had reduced the army to a critical state, and said the armed forces would be modernised -- and reduced -- to cope with their new defensive role.
He added that in this respect the experiences the 16 members of NATO had in likewise slimming down their standing armies would be used as a guide.

"Therefore our western partners have no reason to worry. In particular I can assure them that the Russian nuclear button remains in sure hands and the various suppositions that control of nuclear weapons would be lost are pure investions," Chernomyrdin told the paper.
The Russian Prime Minister was scheduled to meet his Belgian counterpart Jean-Luc Dehaene on Thursday evening, and on Friday he will meet representatives of the armed forces and the king.
